claims.text: The as-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous FCC matrix with minimal secondary phases.
Elevated-temperature degradation in oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by oxide nucleation and growth along grain boundaries.
The governing grain-boundary oxide is primarily aluminum-rich.
Grain-boundary oxides embrittle the boundaries.
Grain-boundary oxides act as stress concentrators that promote intergranular cracking and catastrophic failure.
Oxygen partial pressure or another reactive-species partial pressure can be systematically varied to reveal the governing degradation behavior.
The proposed governing behavior applies over approximately 700–900 °C, where diffusion is activated.
The relevant structural evolution includes formation, growth, and eventual spallation of aluminum-rich or mixed oxide at grain boundaries.
In an oxidizing atmosphere, surface and grain-boundary oxidation produces a protective but brittle aluminum-rich oxide.
Mismatch between the oxide and FCC matrix in thermal or mechanical properties creates stress concentrations as the oxide grows.
Oxide-induced stress concentrations promote intergranular cracking.
In reducing atmospheres, changes in oxide chemistry and kinetics may reduce grain-boundary cohesion and cause failure when a critical oxide-film morphology is reached.
Higher oxygen partial pressure will accelerate grain-boundary oxide growth relative to less oxidizing or reducing exposure.
Higher oxygen partial pressure will increase embrittlement and cause earlier intergranular cracking and failure.
Exposed specimens will develop localized grain-boundary oxide precipitates and deteriorated mechanical properties relative to the as-manufactured state.
The as-manufactured alloy has superior high-temperature mechanical stability under inert conditions.
The hypothesis applies where oxygen activity is sufficient to drive oxidation but insufficient to cause immediate complete surface passivation.
Gas composition is assumed to be the primary degradation variable when processing-related stress concentrators and other factors are held unchanged.
SEM/TEM, EDS, mechanical testing, and fractography can test for correlations among grain-boundary oxidation, mechanical degradation, and intergranular failure.

Failure to observe greater grain-boundary oxidation, embrittlement, and earlier failure at high oxygen partial pressure than under reducing or inert conditions would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
